chunks: Sa'd narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Rifah, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the person whose hand is dyed with henna, if he is able to perform prostration and recitation as well, does he pray with his henna? He said: 'Yes, if his cloth is pure and he is in a state of ablution.'

key_terms.الْمُخْتَضِبِ: One whose hand is dyed with henna

ai.seo_question: Does henna on the hand invalidate prayer in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Rida (AS), the juristic principle of 'ease in hardship' (taysir) is applied to ritual purity, confirming that henna itself is not a barrier to prayer as long as it does not prevent water from reaching the skin during wudu or impede the physical act of sujud. The condition of the cloth being 'pure' (tahira) highlights the distinction between the substance's inherent purity and the ritual state of the covering, reflecting the Usuli focus on removing unnecessary obstacles to worship. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on practicality, ensuring that common practices like henna application do not complicate the validity of salah.
